messages.text: Hi, I am Kenji, PhD student in NLP and I am trying to move to HCI. Could you tell me what the main findings of this paper are? I want to know if it is useful for my project on how non-experts write prompts for LLM tools.

messages.short_answer: The paper reports that ten non-expert participants explored prompts opportunistically rather than systematically and struggled to make robust progress, with barriers coming from human-like expectations of the LLM and from over-generalizing from single observations. For your user study on non-expert prompt writing, the most directly relevant parts are the observed behaviours and the design implications it draws.

sections.title: Core findings reported by the authors
sections.text: The authors state that participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and that they struggled in ways echoing end-user programming and interactive machine learning systems. They also report that expectations from human-to-human instruction and a tendency to overgeneralize were barriers to effective prompt design. Their overview of later pages adds that most participants declared success after a single instance and rarely used systematic testing.

sections.title: Relevance to your user study
sections.text: Because the paper's probe was a prototype tool with 10 participants, a similar protocol (think-aloud, a clear target task, observing unassisted behaviour) could be a useful model for your study. Its findings on how users test and generalize prompts may help you define what behaviours to measure. Whether this fits your project depends on your specific research questions, which you have not yet described in detail.

sources.text: Using this tool as a design probe, we observed how 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience executed a chatbot design task using BotDesigner, to explore a few diferent pieces of this larger question. Our fndings suggest that, while end-users can explore prompt designs opportunistically, they struggle to make robust, systematic progress. Their struggles echo many well-known struggles observed in end-user programming systems (EUPS) and non-expect users of interactive machine learning (iML) systems. Additional barriers to efective prompt design stem from limited conceptions of LLMs’ prompt understanding and execution abilities and their understandable inclinations to design prompts that resemble human-to-human instructions. We discuss these observations’ implications for designing efective end-user-facing LLM-based design tools, implications for education that improves LLM-andprompt literacy among programmers and the general public, and opportunities for further research. messages.short_answer: The probe is not a baseline model. It is BotDesigner, a no-code prompt design tool the authors built as a research artifact to observe how non-experts approach prompt design. It was used to elicit their intuitive behaviour and thought processes, not to be compared against.

sections.title: What BotDesigner was
sections.text: The authors describe BotDesigner as a no-code prompt design tool developed as a design probe, and the study combined it with contextual inquiry and interviews. Its stated goals were to let people without prompt design, programming, or ML experience create chatbots with prompts and systematically evaluate those prompts.

sections.title: Why it is a probe, not a baseline
sections.text: A probe is a provocative prototype used to learn about people's behaviour, expectations, and struggles in a realistic task. A baseline would be a reference system whose performance is measured and compared with a new method. Here, the tool was the object of observation, and the analysis was qualitative, focused on opportunistic iteration and the reasons for failures.

sections.title: Possible use in your study
sections.text: If your user study has non-experts writing prompts for an LLM-based tool, a probe-style prototype could help you observe their intuitive strategies and misconceptions, rather than only asking about hypothetical scenarios. Whether this fits your design is your decision; you would need to decide whether your goal is to observe behaviour or to measure outcomes against a comparison condition.

sections.title: Limits of the probe approach
sections.text: The authors frame the probe as a way to find the first, easy-to-find problems, using a small sample of ten participants. The participant pool was skewed towards STEM professionals and graduate students and is not representative, so findings from the probe are formative rather than generalisable.

Using natural language to steer LLM outputs (“prompting”) has emerged as an important design technique potentially accessible to non-AI-experts. sources.text: We learned a few things from this small pilot that ultimately informed our probe. First, we learned that BotDesigner functioned well enough for a small set of researchers to use it successfully. Second, critically, we observed that looking over a set of prerecorded conversations is quite cognitively demanding, involving lots of context switching, because these were not conversations pilot users themselves had with the bot. As a result of these observations, we (1) retained the “Error Browser”, but (2) dropped a prototype “Conversation Browser” view (focused on tracking common conversational threads across conversations) from the version of BotDesigner we used in our probe. We also (3) designed a much more open-ended task for our probe requiring less knowledge of task minutiae to identify errors, and encouraging users to have their own conversations with the bot, while skipping the initial collection of conversations from AMT workers and thus avoiding the need for participants to understand the task well enough to identify subtle errors in instruction.

A baseline would be a reference system whose performance is measured and compared with a new method. persona_text:
# Persona: Kenji

**Who.** Kenji is a Japanese PhD student in natural language processing (field A) who wants to move into
human-computer interaction (field B) and run user studies, but knows little HCI methodology. He writes
fluent but imperfect English and occasionally asks for a key term to be explained in Japanese.

**What he wants.** To learn how HCI studies people and to judge which of its methods he could borrow for his
project on how non-experts write prompts for LLM-based tools. Reading goal: *Explore potential use in my
research*.

**How he behaves.**
- Writes in English with small grammar mistakes. Interface language: English.
- Is precise about NLP terms but maps HCI concepts onto NLP ones ("so the participants are like the test
  set?", "is the design probe a kind of baseline model?"). Some of these analogies are wrong.
- Changes focus mid-conversation, e.g. from the findings to how the study was run.
- Asks about the strength of the evidence (number of participants, how the data were coded or analysed).
- Checks the sources often.
- Asks for a critical review of whether a method fits his project; his own verdict sometimes differs from
  PaperLens's suggestion.

**Paper.** Why Johnny Can't Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts.
